title: Westbrook School Committee — Finance Committee Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)
fields.Packet: No agenda was published for this meeting (checked westbrookschools.org, 2026-10-24).

packetNote: No agenda was published for this meeting (checked westbrookschools.org, 2026-10-24).
note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Members reviewed the budget in this third consecutive fiscal year 2027 (FY27) cost-center budget review session; no votes were taken. For complete context, nuance, and anything not covered, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: Finance Committee Chair Noreen Poitras, School Committee Chair Andrea Mancuso, School Committee Vice Chair Katy Rice, Erin Cavallaro, Dr. Flynn Ross. Not stated on the recording: Allison Brunette, Brooke Reed.

blocks.x: School Nutrition: Fully Self-Funded, New Education Coordinator

Director Mary Emerson confirmed the program is fully funded by federal/state meal reimbursements and puts no local taxpayer dollars on the table. The budget proposes a new Nutrition Education Coordinator (~$64,046 net of expiring FoodCorps funding it partly replaces). The program recently won the Southern Maine school-nutrition cook-off, advancing to the state competition.
Staff to post on the website (or email) the salary and benefit sheets for the enterprise accounts, which were left out of the printed budget book.
Athletics & Activities: New Playoff/Officiating Costs, Software Review

Director Mark Campbell (first budget cycle) reported 511 high school and 405 middle school athlete participations, plus 26 and 12 clubs respectively, and flagged a 15-point gender participation gap he is working to track more precisely. New costs include officiating fee increases tied to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and, for the first time, a budgeted line for playoff-game officiating/travel (five playoff games hosted this year already). Campbell said the athletic-management software, which he is testing against an alternative, could yield savings of up to about $3,000.

Campbell to work with Director Lombardo on a breakdown of school use of the athletic fields and the cost of maintaining them, for a Friday meeting with City Hall on the $121,000 charge. The athletic-management software line went on the revisit list, and staff are to bring a revenue list (including athletic gate receipts) the next night.
“This $121,000 has not sat super comfortably with the committee...we want to understand what is the real need versus what is showing up in our budget books.”
blocks.cite: Andrea Mancuso, School Committee Chair (on the city's $121,000 athletic-field maintenance charge)

blocks.x: Budget Overview: Restored Professional Development/Library Lines, ~$160K Utility Savings

Principal Dr. Borsaw (new this year) presented a budget restoring previously zeroed-out professional development and library equipment lines and expects about 22 more students next year (mostly incoming fifth graders) with no new classroom staffing request. The committee noted roughly $160,000 in utility savings at the school.

On the revisit list: the $23,000 bathroom fix, the middle and high school School Resource Officer lines, a contract line tied to Nelson Property Services, health insurance, substitutes, and contingency (with budget-to-actual figures for recent years).

“For $30 a student, we can fix the bathrooms at the middle school and make children comfortable...We spend more money on athletic department software than it would take to fix an entire grade span's bathrooms that the kids are feeling so deeply about...I will have a hard time supporting this budget if we don't fix the bathroom issue at the middle school.”
blocks.cite: Andrea Mancuso, School Committee Chair (on inadequate middle school bathroom privacy, a $23,000 fix not in the budget)

blocks.x: “Coming from New York City, I was in a school that had security...metal detectors at every door...they moved it to a small school model, got rid of all the SROs...achievement went up, discipline went down...it's well documented that SROs do not contribute to the educational setting.”
blocks.cite: Dr. Flynn Ross, School Committee member (on School Resource Officer funding)

blocks.x: A Multi-Year English Teacher Request, Compass Program Relocation

Principal Jeff Garrett reported strong outcomes (38% of students in early college/Advanced Placement (AP)/dual enrollment) and renewed the school's multi-year request for a new English teacher — seven teachers currently cover roughly

700 students, versus eight in math, with English the only subject required all four years and some sections approaching 25 students. Also proposed: relocating the school's Compass alternative-education program (about 15 students) from a separate outbuilding into renovated space inside the main building, and a technology shift from MacBooks toward iPads following a fall pilot. Both the high school's and middle school's School Resource Officer (SRO) funding and the Compass relocation were added to the revisit list. The library equipment line, zeroed out in past years, was restored, and the IXL software line was corrected on the spot for a savings of about $4,646.
The Compass relocation went on the revisit list, with costs requested with and without a bathroom. The committee also asked for current and projected class-size data across all three grade spans.
WRVC: Two New Programs, Enrollment Growth, Aging-Building Concerns

Westbrook Regional Vocational Center (WRVC) Director Gloria Noyes reported enrollment up 44–50 students despite closing the commercial driver's license (CDL) program, driven by active recruitment. The budget funds two new programs — a Career and Technical Education (CTE) Exploratory Program and a Cooperative Education internship program — both expected to further grow enrollment and state subsidy. Noyes flagged aging-building issues at the roughly 30-year-old facility (roof leaks, inconsistent temperatures, no secure entry vestibule); staff said the entry-security issue might be handled within the operating budget, and the building is on the list for capital-planning talks with the City.
Staff to provide a crosswalk showing where WRVC's reorganized budget lines moved.
Adult Education: Top-Performing Program, About $376K Local Share

Director Jen Brooks reported the state's third-largest adult education program, recognized this year as a top performer in Maine, serving 576 students (up nearly 7%). Outside revenue (workforce-training revenue, grants, and a state subsidy up 9.88% to $165,122) covers about $292,000 of the program's roughly $668,500 cost, leaving a local share of roughly $376,310. The budget expands digital literacy instruction for workforce readiness and pilots an online English platform (Burlington English), which Brooks said January's immigration-enforcement events showed the program needs in order to be “ready for anything.”
Staff to report, for the revisit list, on community-center resources that support the adult education program's work with new Mainers.
